# Idli Batter (2kg batch)

## Method

Wash and soak the rice and the urad dal separately for 4 to 6 hours, with the
fenugreek seeds in the dal bowl. Grind the dal first with ice-cold water until
light, fluffy and tripled in volume — it should hold a soft peak. Grind the
rice to a fine rava-like texture, slightly grainy between the fingers. Combine
both with the rock salt and mix by hand for a full 2 minutes; the warmth of
your hand kick-starts the wild fermentation. Ferment 8 to 12 hours at 28–32°C
until doubled and domed. Do not stir the risen batter. Scoop gently into
greased idli moulds and steam 12 minutes; rest 2 minutes before unmoulding.

# Idli Batter (2kg batch)

## Ingredients

| Ingredient | Weight | % of rice |
|---|---|---|
| Idli rice (parboiled) | 1000g | 100% |
| Whole white urad dal | 250g | 25% |
| Fenugreek seeds | 10g | 1% |
| Rock salt | 20g | 2% |
| Water for grinding | ~720g | 72% |

Rice to dal ratio: 4:1. Final batter weight: approximately 2kg.

# Crisp Dosa Batter

## Method

Soak rice, urad dal, chana dal and fenugreek together for 5 hours; soak the
poha separately for the last 30 minutes. Grind everything to a smooth, flowing
batter — thinner than idli batter — adding water a little at a time. Stir in
the salt and ferment 10 to 14 hours at 26–30°C until risen by half and sour-
smelling. Thin with water to pouring-cream consistency. Heat a cast-iron tawa
until a water drop dances, wipe with an oiled onion half, pour a ladleful in
the centre and spiral outward with the ladle base to a thin, even round.
Drizzle the edges with gingelly oil and cook until deep gold and crisp; a
proper dosa releases itself from the pan.

# Idli Batter (2kg batch)

Percentages are relative to the rice weight (100%).

# Idli Batter (2kg batch)

## Allergen note

Naturally vegan and gluten-free. If adding asafoetida (hing), check the label —
most Indian brands are bound with wheat flour.

# Appam (lace-edged fermented rice hoppers)

## Ingredients

| Ingredient | Weight | % of rice |
|---|---|---|
| Raw rice (pachari), soaked | 500g | 100% |
| Cooked rice | 100g | 20% |
| Fresh thick coconut milk | 400g | 80% |
| Fresh toddy (or 1g instant yeast + 10g sugar in warm water) | 100g | 20% |
| Sugar | 15g | 3% |
| Fine sea salt | 7g | 1.4% |

# Appam (lace-edged fermented rice hoppers)

## Method

Soak the raw rice 4 hours, then grind with the cooked rice and half the
coconut milk to a completely smooth batter. Stir in the toddy (or the yeast
mixture) and the sugar, and ferment 8 hours at room temperature until bubbly
and risen. Just before cooking, stir in the remaining coconut milk and the 7g
fine sea salt; the batter should coat a spoon thinly. Heat an appachatti,
pour in a small ladleful, and immediately lift and swirl the pan in one full
circle so the batter climbs the walls — this makes the crisp lace edge with
the soft, spongy centre. Cover and cook 2 minutes; the appam is done when the
edges release and the centre springs back.

# Thayir — Homemade Curd (set overnight)

## Method

Bring the milk just to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes to concentrate it
slightly — this gives a thicker set. Cool to 40–43°C: the milk should feel
distinctly warm, not hot, on a clean fingertip held for ten seconds. Whisk
the starter curd until smooth, stir it through the milk, cover, and leave
completely undisturbed for 6 to 8 hours at around 30°C. In cold weather, set
the pot inside a switched-off oven with the light on, or wrap it in a thick
towel next to a hot-water bottle. The curd is set when it jiggles as one mass
and the surface releases a little clear whey. Refrigerate immediately once
set; over-fermenting at room temperature turns it sharply sour by evening.
Save 30g as the starter for tomorrow's batch.

# Ragi Koozh (fermented finger-millet porridge)

## Method

Whisk the ragi flour into 500g of the water until lump-free, and leave the
slurry overnight — 10 to 12 hours — in a clay pot at room temperature to
ferment; by morning it smells pleasantly sour and shows fine bubbles. Cook
the broken rice in the remaining 1000g of water until completely soft. Stir
the fermented ragi slurry into the simmering rice in a steady stream,
whisking constantly, and cook 8 to 10 minutes until the porridge thickens
and turns glossy chocolate-brown. Add the rock salt at the end. Cool to
lukewarm and thin with water to a drinkable consistency. Traditionally
enjoyed the next day, when a second, gentler fermentation in the pot deepens
the sourness — this is summer street food, sold cold from mud pots.

# Ragi Koozh (fermented finger-millet porridge)

Vegan and gluten-free as written. Often served with buttermilk stirred in —
that version contains dairy.

# Kadumanga Achar (Kerala fermented tender mango pickle)

## Ingredients

| Ingredient | Weight | % of mango |
|---|---|---|
| Tender baby mangoes (kannimanga), whole | 1000g | 100% |
| Crystal sea salt | 150g | 15% |
| Kashmiri chilli powder | 50g | 5% |
| Gingelly (sesame) oil | 60g | 6% |
| Mustard seeds | 10g | 1% |
| Fenugreek powder, roasted | 5g | 0.5% |
| Asafoetida (hing) | 3g | 0.3% |

# Kadumanga Achar (Kerala fermented tender mango pickle)

## Method

Wipe the mangoes dry — no water must touch them at any stage. Layer them
with the crystal salt in a sterilised bharani (ceramic pickle jar), close,
and shake once daily. Over 10 to 14 days the salt draws out the mango's own
brine and the fruit ferments in it, turning olive-drab and pleasantly tangy.
Then heat the gingelly oil, crackle the mustard seeds, switch off the heat,
and stir in the chilli powder, fenugreek powder and asafoetida. Cool the
spiced oil completely and fold it through the mangoes and their brine.
Return everything to the bharani. The pickle is eatable in a week but
matures over a month; it keeps a year at room temperature if only dry
spoons ever enter the jar.

wheat flour — use a certified gluten-free hing or omit it for gluten-free
diets; as written this card is NOT gluten-free.

# Thayir — Homemade Curd (set overnight)

## Method

Bring the milk just to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes to concentrate it
slightly — this gives a thicker set. Cool to 40–43°C: the milk should feel
distinctly warm, not hot, on a clean fingertip held for ten seconds. Whisk
the starter curd until smooth, stir it through the milk, cover, and leave
completely undisturbed for 6 to 8 hours at around 30°C. In cold weather, set
the pot inside a switched-off oven with the light on, or wrap it in a thick
towel next to a hot-water bottle. The curd is set when it jiggles as one mass
and the surface releases a little clear whey. Refrigerate immediately once
set; over-fermenting at room temperature turns it sharply sour by evening.
Save 30g as the starter for tomorrow's batch.

# Appam (lace-edged fermented rice hoppers)

## Method

Soak the raw rice 4 hours, then grind with the cooked rice and half the
coconut milk to a completely smooth batter. Stir in the toddy (or the yeast
mixture) and the sugar, and ferment 8 hours at room temperature until bubbly
and risen. Just before cooking, stir in the remaining coconut milk and the 7g

edges release and the centre springs back.

# Thayir — Homemade Curd (set overnight)

## Method

Bring the milk just to a boil, then simmer 5 minutes to concentrate it
slightly — this gives a thicker set. Cool to 40–43°C: the milk should feel
distinctly warm, not hot, on a clean fingertip held for ten seconds. Whisk
the starter curd until smooth, stir it through the milk, cover, and leave
completely undisturbed for 6 to 8 hours at around 30°C. In cold weather, set
the pot inside a switched-off oven with the light on, or wrap it in a thick
towel next to a hot-water bottle. The curd is set when it jiggles as one mass
and the surface releases a little clear whey. Refrigerate immediately once
set; over-fermenting at room temperature turns it sharply sour by evening.
Save 30g as the starter for tomorrow's batch.
